topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. Equilibrium carries 6 to 8 marks a paper: a whole question when four forces act at a point, and the opening parts of the forces question otherwise. The reports call it a good differentiator, and the marks turn on whether a complete equation is written rather than on the arithmetic.
mustMemorise: In equilibrium the resultant is zero, so the total in each of two perpendicular directions is zero
At rest, held still and constant velocity all mean the forces balance
Every force with a part in a direction appears in that direction's equation
On a slope, resolve along the slope and at right angles to it
The normal reaction on a slope is mg cos of the slope's angle, always less than the weight
Friction holds a body still on a rough slope, acting up it and matching mg sin of the angle
notOnThisSpec: Limiting equilibrium, the coefficient of friction and F = μR: a frictional force is given, or is found from the balance itself
More than four separate forces, which the Teacher Guidance rules out
Equilibrium of a rigid body by moments: that is the uniform-rod topic, not this one
Lami's theorem and the triangle of forces
g = 9.8 m/s²: this unit takes g = 10 m/s², as the front page of every FM2 paper states

sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2. Equilibrium is examined as a whole question when four forces act at a point (Summer 2024 Q3: 3 marks for each of the two unknowns, and Summer 2026 Q2 in the same shape) and as the opening parts of a longer forces question otherwise (Summer 2023 Q3(i) and (ii), 2 marks each; Summer 2025 Q6(ii), 2 marks; Summer 2019 Q3(ii), 4 marks). The schemes give M for naming the direction and forming an equation, MW for the equation itself and W for the value, with follow-through into the later parts.
traps: Vertical equilibrium not recognised at all, so no equation is written (Summer 2019 Q3(ii))
An equation with two terms where three or four belong (Summer 2019 Q3(ii), Summer 2024 Q3)
The reaction written down as the weight, or as a single component, with no resolving (Summer 2023 Q3(i))
A zero acceleration not understood, so an acceleration is hunted for where the motion is steady (Summer 2023 Q3(ii))
One resolved component written down and nothing equated, so the later marks cannot be reached (Summer 2024 Q3)
Sine and cosine interchanged when resolving on a slope (Summer 2025 Q6(ii))

Because the tension is too small to matter here

steps.working: Check: $124.74$ N is less than the weight of $140$ N, as it must be on a slope.
steps.decision: A reaction larger than the weight would mean the cosine of the angle was greater than one, so this check catches a swapped ratio.

workedExamples.stem:
A particle at $O$ is held in equilibrium by three forces: $20$ N acting horizontally to the right, $15$ N acting vertically downwards, and a force of $P$ N acting at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, to the left.

(i) Calculate the value of $P$.
(ii) Calculate the value of $\theta$. Round to 2 decimal places.

figure.alt: A particle at O held in equilibrium by three forces: 20 N horizontally to the right, 15 N vertically downwards, and a force of P newtons acting up and to the left at an angle to the horizontal that has to be found.

steps.decision: The third force is the only one with an unknown direction, so write its two components as $P\cos\theta$ and $P\sin\theta$ and let the equations find them.
The second equation comes from the other direction. Two equations, two unknowns.
$P\cos\theta$ and $P\sin\theta$ are the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle whose longest side is $P$, so Pythagoras gives $P^2 = 20^2 + 15^2$.
Dividing the two equations removes $P$ instead, leaving the angle on its own.

items.stem: A particle is in equilibrium under four forces. What is the resultant of the four forces?

options.feedback: Nothing is left over, which is exactly why the particle does not accelerate.
Every force takes part in the balance, so none of them survives on its own.

options.text: the total of the four sizes
options.feedback: That totals the sizes and ignores the directions, which is what makes them cancel.

options.text: it cannot be found without the mass

items.stem: A crate is dragged across a floor at a constant velocity of $3$ m/s. What is true of the forces on it?

options.text: they balance, because the acceleration is zero
options.feedback: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so $F = ma$ gives a resultant of zero.

options.text: they do not balance, because the crate is moving
options.feedback: Motion at a steady speed needs nothing left over; it is changing speed that does.

options.text: the driving force must be larger than the friction
options.feedback: A larger driving force would speed the crate up, so the velocity would not be constant.

options.text: there is not enough information to say
options.feedback: Constant velocity is all the information needed: it sets the resultant to zero.

items.skill: The reaction when a rope lifts
items.stem: A block of weight $70$ N rests on a table while a rope pulls it with a vertical component of $20$ N upwards. Which equation gives the normal reaction?

options.feedback: The table and the rope together hold the weight up, so their totals match it.
That leaves the rope out. The reports describe candidates giving the reaction as the weight with no resolving done.
That leaves the weight out and keeps only the rope.
The rope pulls upwards, the same way as the reaction, so it takes work away from the table rather than adding to it.

items.stem: A box of weight $150$ N is held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at $30°$ to the horizontal by a rope parallel to the slope. What is the normal reaction?

options.feedback: Only the part of the weight pressing into the surface has to be balanced.
The reaction equals the weight only on a horizontal surface, where nothing else is vertical.
That is the component down the slope, which friction or a rope has to balance instead.
Tangent compares the two components and cannot give either from the weight.

items.skill: A component is not an equation
items.stem: A candidate resolving a force in an equilibrium question writes $25\sin 40°$ and stops. How is that marked?

options.text: a method mark for one correct resolved component, and no more
options.feedback: The schemes allow the first mark for a correct component; the marks after it are for the equation it belongs in.

options.text: full marks, because the resolving is right
options.feedback: The question asks for a value, and a value needs the complete equation.
A correct component is worth something, which is why it is always worth writing down.

options.text: a method mark only if the answer that follows is right
options.feedback: A method mark stands on its own, whatever comes after it.

items.stem: Three forces have vertical parts: a reaction $R$ upwards, a pull of $22\sin 36°$ upwards and a weight of $75$ N downwards. Which vertical equation is complete?

options.feedback: All three vertical parts appear, and the two upward ones together match the weight.
The weight has dropped out. This exact two-term shape is the one the reports single out.
The pull has dropped out, so the table is being asked to hold the whole weight.
The pull acts upwards, so it helps the reaction rather than adding to what it must support.

items.stem: A crate of weight $90$ N rests on a rough slope inclined at $25°$, with nothing attached to it. What is the force due to friction?

options.feedback: Friction is the only force along the slope, so it matches the component of the weight pulling the crate down it.
The size is right, but friction opposes the way the crate would slide, which is downwards.
That is the component pressing into the slope, which the normal reaction balances.
That is the whole weight. Only the part along the slope has to be held.

items.skill: Choosing the two directions on a slope
items.stem: Which pair of directions makes an equilibrium problem on a slope shortest to solve?

options.text: along the slope and at right angles to it
options.feedback: The reaction and any rope along the slope then need no resolving, leaving only the weight to split.
That works, but then both the reaction and the tension have to be resolved instead of one force.
That can be solved, but the two directions are not at right angles, so every force has to be resolved into both and the working grows.
Two different directions do give two equations, but unless they are at right angles each force has to be resolved awkwardly; perpendicular ones keep every equation short.

parts.stem:
A crate of mass $12$ kg is held at rest on a smooth ramp inclined at $20°$ to the horizontal by a rope lying along the ramp.

Calculate the tension in the rope. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving along the ramp: $T = 120\sin 20°$

hints: Work out the weight first.
Resolve along the ramp.
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= 12 \times 10 = 120$ N. Resolving along the ramp, $T = 120\sin 20° = 41.04$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $120\cos 20°$, the component pressing into the ramp. Along the ramp is opposite the angle, so it takes the sine.
That is the whole weight. Only the part of it acting along the ramp has to be held by the rope.

parts.stem:
Calculate the normal reaction of the ramp on the crate. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving at right angles to the ramp: $R = 120\cos 20°$

hints: The rope lies along the ramp, so it has no part at right angles to it.
parts.workedSolution: Resolving at right angles to the ramp, $R = 120\cos 20° = 112.76$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reaction on a horizontal surface. On a ramp only part of the weight presses into the surface, so the reaction is smaller.
That is the component along the ramp, which the rope holds. Into the ramp sits beside the angle and takes the cosine.

parts.stem:
A crate of mass $11$ kg rests on a rough slope inclined at $16°$ to the horizontal, with nothing attached to it.

Calculate the force due to friction on the crate. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving along the slope: $F = 110\sin 16°$

hints: Which force is the only one lying along the slope?
The crate is at rest, so the forces along the slope balance.
parts.workedSolution: The crate is at rest, so resolving along the slope, $F = 110\sin 16° = 30.32$ N, acting up the slope.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $110\cos 16°$, which is what the normal reaction balances. Friction lies along the slope and takes the sine.
That is the whole weight. Friction only has to balance the part of it that pulls the crate down the slope.

parts.stem:
Calculate the normal reaction of the slope on the crate. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: resolving at right angles to the slope: $R = 110\cos 16°$

hints: Friction lies along the slope, so it has no part at right angles to it.

hints: Write the unknown force's two components as $P\cos\theta$ and $P\sin\theta$.
The two components are the shorter sides of a right-angled triangle with $P$ as its longest side.
parts.workedSolution: Horizontally: $P\cos\theta = 45$. Vertically: $P\sin\theta = 28$. These are the shorter sides of a right-angled triangle with longest side $P$, so by Pythagoras $P^2 = 45^2 + 28^2 = 2809$ and $P = 53$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That totals the two sizes. They act at right angles, so the force that balances them comes from Pythagoras instead.
That is $P^2$, so all three method marks (M) are safe. The square root is the last step.

parts.stem:

$\tan\theta = \dfrac{28}{45}$

hints: Dividing the two equations removes $P$.
parts.workedSolution: Dividing the vertical equation by the horizontal one, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{28}{45}$, so $\theta = 31.89°$.

commonErrors.feedback: That fraction is the wrong way up and gives the angle with the vertical. The question measures $\theta$ from the horizontal.
That is the size of the force from part (a), not an angle. The angle comes from the ratio of the two components.

findTheMistake.stem: Eoin is finding the normal reaction on a block of weight $75$ N resting on a rough table. A rope pulls the block at $36°$ to the table with a force of $22$ N, and the block does not move. His working:
studentWorking: the block does not move, so the vertical forces balance
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 has only two terms where three belong. Three forces have a vertical part: the reaction upwards, the rope's $22\sin 36°$ upwards, and the weight of $75$ N downwards. Leaving the weight out makes the equation say the rope alone is being balanced.
findTheMistake.feedback: Naming the direction and saying the forces balance is the method, and it earns the method mark (M). Before writing an equation, list every force that has a part in that direction: three here, so three terms. The examiners describe the two-term equation as very common in this kind of question.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife is finding the normal reaction on a box of mass $11$ kg held at rest on a smooth slope inclined at $24°$ by a rope parallel to the slope. Her working:
studentWorking: the box is at rest, so the reaction balances the weight
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 skips the resolving. The reaction is at right angles to the slope and the weight is vertical, so they are not in the same direction and cannot simply match. Only the component of the weight pressing into the slope, $110\cos 24°$, is balanced by $R$.
correction: resolving at right angles to the slope: $R = 110\cos 24°$
findTheMistake.feedback: Turning the mass into a weight is worth the first mark, and it is right here. Two forces balance only when they lie along the same line: check that before equating anything, and on a slope the reaction and the weight never do.

findTheMistake.stem: Dara is working with a crate that is being dragged across a floor at a constant velocity of $4$ m/s. His working:
studentWorking: the crate is moving, so the forces do not balance
the pull must be larger than the friction
so there is a resultant force and the crate accelerates
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 reads movement as a sign of a resultant force. What creates a resultant is a change of velocity, not velocity itself. The velocity here is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the forces do balance.
correction: the velocity is constant, so the acceleration is zero

prompts.prompt: What does it mean for a particle to be in equilibrium?
prompts.answer: The resultant of the forces on it is zero, so it has no acceleration.

prompts.prompt: How many equations does an equilibrium problem give you, and where do they come from?
prompts.answer: Two, one from each of two perpendicular directions, with the total in each set to zero.

prompts.prompt: A candidate writes one correct resolved component and stops. What is still needed?
prompts.answer: An equation with every force that has a part in that direction, set equal to zero.

prompts.prompt: Which three phrases in a question all mean the forces balance?
prompts.answer: At rest, held still, and moving with constant velocity.

prompts.prompt: Which two directions make an equilibrium problem on a slope shortest?
prompts.answer: Along the slope and at right angles to it, because only the weight then needs resolving.

prompts.prompt: A box of weight W rests on a slope inclined at an angle. What is the normal reaction?
prompts.answer: W cosine of the angle, because only that component of the weight presses into the surface.

prompts.prompt: Why is the normal reaction not equal to the weight when a rope pulls a block at an angle?
prompts.answer: Part of the pull is upwards, so the table supports less than the whole weight.

prompts.prompt: A crate rests on a rough slope with nothing attached. Which force holds it there?
prompts.answer: The force due to friction, acting up the slope.

prompts.prompt: What is the commonest shape of a wrong equilibrium equation?
prompts.answer: One with two terms where three or four belong, because a force has been left out.

prompts.prompt: Three forces hold a particle still and two of them are perpendicular. How do you find the third?
prompts.answer: It balances the resultant of the other two, so its magnitude comes from Pythagoras and its direction is opposite.

The note's own examples: 140 sin 27 = 63.56, 140 cos 27 = 124.74, 70 sin 18 = 21.63, 70 cos 18 = 66.57, and 20 N with 15 N giving 25 N at 36.87°. Twins: 90 - 40 sin 35 = 67.06, 130 sin 22 = 48.7, sqrt(225 + 64) = 17. Every distractor is produced by executing a wrongly shaped balance (a term dropped, a sign kept, a ratio swapped, a force left unresolved) through the same route, and re-checked against the published JSON by verify-published.mjs.
